screens.title: Network File Systems: NFS and Samba
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we explore two essential network file systems you will use as an LFCE: NFS for Unix-native sharing, and Samba to serve Windows clients. You will learn practical server and client steps, how to secure shares, and how to diagnose common permission and connectivity problems. NFSv4 simplifies firewall configuration by using port 2049 and offers stateful behavior; Samba implements SMB/CIFS so Linux servers can present Windows-style file and print services. We'll walk through configuration files you must master: /etc/exports for NFS and /etc/samba/smb. conf for Samba, plus the key commands like exportfs and smbpasswd. You will also see concrete examples for public and secured shares, mounting commands and fstab entries, and the security tradeoffs of options such as no_root_squash. Understanding these tradeoffs matters because misconfigured network shares open data to unauthorized users or can break applications that expect root access. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to configure a working NFSv4 export, create a Samba share for mixed environments, tune basic performance options, and troubleshoot the most common errors. Consider which protocol fits each workload and what controls you’ll apply in production.

screens.title: NFS vs Samba — Choosing the right protocol
screens.narratorSegment: Begin by understanding the roles each protocol plays. NFS is designed for Unix-like systems and provides a native filesystem semantics familiar to Linux administrators. It tends to be faster in homogeneous Linux fleets and integrates with Unix permissions, UID/GID mapping, and advanced features like Kerberos for strong authentication. Samba implements the SMB/CIFS protocol to serve Windows clients. Samba exposes shares that Windows expects—network drive mapping, Windows ACLs if configured, and simple guest access. A practical decision rule is: if your clients are primarily Linux servers or you need POSIX semantics, favor NFSv4; if you must support Windows workstations or mixed environments, use Samba. There are important contrasts to watch for. NFSv4 uses port 2049 and can be integrated with id mapping and Kerberos, which changes how permissions are enforced. Samba uses ports 139 and 445 and relies on smbpasswd or domain membership for authentication. Misconceptions often arise: some assume NFS is always insecure because it uses IP-based access by default; while true for simple setups, NFSv4 can be integrated with Kerberos for mutual authentication and encryption. Another misconception is that Samba is only for Windows; Samba serves Linux clients too via CIFS mounts. When planning, consider client mix, performance needs, and the authentication model you require.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › NFS vs Samba
NFSv4 — Unix-native
Key traits: POSIX semantics, optimized for Linux servers, uses port 2049, supports Kerberos, and relies on /etc/exports for access control.
Best for homogeneous Linux server clusters and performance-sensitive workloads.
Integrates with UID/GID mapping and Kerberos for enterprise security.
Example export line:
/srv/nfs/data 192.168.1.100(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash)
Samba — Windows interoperability
Key traits: implements SMB/CIFS to serve Windows clients, configure shares in /etc/samba/smb.conf, supports guest shares and authenticated users with smbpasswd or Active Directory domain membership.
Best when Windows users must map network drives, or mixed clients require SMB features.
Support for guest shares and authenticated shares via smbpasswd or domain integration.
Example smb.conf share:
[public]
    comment = Public Samba Share
    path = /srv/samba/public
    browseable = yes
    read only = no
    guest ok = yes
Misconception
NFS is not inherently insecure. While simple setups rely on IP control, NFSv4 can use Kerberos for proper authentication and encryption.
Pro tip
Match protocol to client capabilities. If a Windows user must edit files, Samba is the smoother user experience.
Check
Ask which authentication model you need: IP-based, local accounts, Kerberos, or AD domain join.

screens.title: Set up an NFSv4 server
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up an NFSv4 server is a short sequence of repeatable steps you will use in production. Start by installing the server package: on Debian/Ubuntu use the nfs-kernel-server package; on RHEL/CentOS use nfs-utils. Create a directory you intend to share, for example /srv/nfs/shared_data, and set ownership and permissions appropriate to the workload. The core configuration lives in /etc/exports. Each export line defines the path, the allowed clients, and options such as rw, sync, no_subtree_check, and root_squash/no_root_squash. After editing /etc/exports run exportfs -ra to reload export rules without restarting the server, and use systemctl restart nfs-server to restart the NFS service if needed. Open the NFS port in your firewall so authorized clients can reach port 2049. A concrete example: to share with a single client for read/write and allow root privileges you might use /srv/nfs/shared_data client_IP(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash), but remember this allows client root to act as server root for that export and should be used only for trusted clients. Think of these steps as a safe checklist you will repeat: install, create, configure, export, and verify. Set up an NFSv4 server means install server packages, create the shared path, configure /etc/exports, reload exports with exportfs -ra, restart services if required, and open port 2049.. In practical terms, install packages, create exports, and apply them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › NFS Server Setup
Step-by-step
  1. Install server packages: apt install nfs-kernel-server or yum install nfs-utils.
  2. Create the share directory and set permissions.
  3. Edit /etc/exports with appropriate client and options.
  4. Run sudo exportfs -ra and restart the NFS server if needed.
  5. Open firewall port 2049 for trusted clients.
Concrete permissions example
sudo mkdir -p /srv/nfs/shared_data
sudo chown nobody:nogroup /srv/nfs/shared_data && sudo chmod 777 /srv/nfs/shared_data
# /etc/exports
/srv/nfs/shared_data 192.168.1.100(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash)

sudo exportfs -ra
sudo systemctl restart nfs-server
Explanation and risks
no_root_squash allows client root to retain root privileges on the export. Only enable for trusted clients and specific application requirements.
sync guarantees data written to disk before returning; it increases safety but reduces write performance.

screens.title: Understanding /etc/exports options
screens.narratorSegment: The /etc/exports file defines what a server shares and how clients may interact with those shares. Each line names a directory and one or more client specifications with options. Common options you will use immediately include rw for read/write, sync to force writes to disk before confirming to the client, no_subtree_check to avoid subtree permission checks for moved files, and root_squash which maps client root to an anonymous user on the server. That last option is particularly important: by default root_squash enhances server safety by preventing a root user on a client from having root privileges on the server. If an application on the client requires root-level access to the exported files, administrators may use no_root_squash, but they must do so only for trusted clients and after considering other protections like Kerberos and firewall controls. A typical production export will limit allowed clients by IP and avoid giving blanket access to all addresses. Remember to run exportfs -ra after editing /etc/exports to apply rules immediately. Misconfigurations often come from overly permissive client wildcards or forgetting to reload exports after changes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › /etc/exports Options
Common options and meaning
  • rw — allow read and write access to clients.
  • sync — server writes to disk before replying to client; safer but slower.
  • no_subtree_check — skip subtree checks when directories move; improves reliability for big exports.
  • root_squash / no_root_squash — control whether client root is mapped to anonymous user; root_squash is safer.
Example (server trusts single client):
/srv/nfs/data 192.168.1.100(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash)
Security guidance
Prefer limiting clients by IP rather than using wildcards in production. Use root_squash unless a trusted workload explicitly requires no_root_squash.
Combine export restrictions with filesystem permissions and, where needed, Kerberos to enforce identity rather than IP alone.
Common mistake
Forgetting exportfs -ra after editing /etc/exports causes the server to continue using the older rules.

screens.title: Exporting shares and server lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: After editing /etc/exports, the exportfs command synchronizes the kernel's export table with your configuration. The command sudo exportfs -ra re-exports all entries and applies changes immediately; it is a lightweight alternative to restarting the entire NFS service. In cases where the NFS server package or kernel module needs a restart, use systemctl restart nfs-server. For firewall configuration ensure that port 2049 is reachable from trusted clients. If using UFW, a simple rule might be sudo ufw allow from to any port nfs; with firewalld use sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=nfs and reload. Remember that older NFS versions used multiple RPC ports, but NFSv4 consolidates most traffic over 2049, simplifying firewall rules. After exporting, verify using sudo exportfs -v to list exported directories and options, and test mounts from a client. A common operational pitfall is reloading exports but forgetting the firewall rule, which leaves clients unable to connect even though the export exists. The operational checklist is: edit exports, run exportfs -ra, verify with exportfs -v, open firewall, and test the client mount. Exporting shares and server lifecycle means use exportfs -ra to apply /etc/exports changes, open port 2049 for trusted clients, and verify exports with exportfs -v before testing client mounts.. In practical terms, using exportfs, systemctl, and firewall rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Commands to know
sudo exportfs -ra       # reload exports
sudo exportfs -v         # show active exports
sudo systemctl restart nfs-server
Use exportfs -ra to apply edits. Restart the service only when necessary. Verify active exports before client testing.
Firewall rules
NFSv4 uses port 2049, so allow that port for trusted hosts. Example UFW rule: sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port nfs. With firewalld use the nfs service plugin and reload the configuration to apply it.
Check

screens.title: Mounting NFS shares and fstab automation
screens.narratorSegment: On the client side, mount an NFSv4 export using the mount command with type nfs4. After installing the client package (nfs-common on Debian or nfs-utils on RHEL), create a mount point such as /mnt/nfs_client and run sudo mount -t nfs4 :/srv/nfs/shared_data /mnt/nfs_client. Verify the mount with df -h or mount. To test write access create a file on the mount and confirm it appears on the server. For persistent mounts add an entry to /etc/fstab using the nfs4 filesystem type, for example: :/srv/nfs/shared_data /mnt/nfs_client nfs4 defaults 0 0. Be careful: an invalid fstab entry can delay boot if the server is unavailable; consider using the noauto,x-systemd. automount or _netdev options where appropriate. A common issue is permission denied after a successful mount: this is often due to root_squash, mismatched UID/GID between client and server, or filesystem permissions on the exported directory. Use id mapping services like idmapd for NFSv4 to help with user mapping, or ensure consistent POSIX IDs across hosts for predictable ownership behavior. Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Mounting NFS
Quick terminal steps
# Install client
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nfs-common

# Create mount point and mount
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs_client
sudo mount -t nfs4 192.168.1.10:/srv/nfs/shared_data /mnt/nfs_client

# Verify
df -h /mnt/nfs_client
# create a file to test
sudo touch /mnt/nfs_client/test_file_from_client.txt
Persistent mounts
Add to /etc/fstab for auto-mounting, but prefer options that avoid blocking boot if the server is down.

screens.title: Performance tuning: NFS and Samba
screens.narratorSegment: Performance tuning for NFS and Samba focuses on balancing throughput and safety. For NFS tuning, client mount options rsize and wsize control the read and write block sizes; larger values can improve throughput on reliable networks. The sync option in an export forces data to disk before acknowledging writes, which ensures integrity but reduces write performance. The async option increases speed but risks data loss on a server crash. For Samba tuning, socket options like TCP_NODELAY, SO_RCVBUF, and SO_SNDBUF can help when you need to tweak network buffering; parameters like min receivefile size and getwd cache also influence performance. Across both systems network factors — latency, bandwidth, and NIC configuration — often dominate. Practical optimizations include using dedicated network interfaces for storage traffic, enabling jumbo frames where the network supports them, and isolating storage traffic from general-purpose networks. Always benchmark changes in a controlled environment; apply one change at a time and measure throughput and latency. A common pitfall is turning on async for NFS without understanding the crash recovery implications. When in doubt, prefer safe defaults and tune only after profiling real workloads.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to diagnose them
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting network file systems starts with a small checklist. If a client cannot mount a share, verify network reachability and firewall rules first. For NFS, ensure port 2049 is reachable and that exportfs -v shows the export. If mounts succeed but reads or writes fail with permission denied, check root_squash behavior and UID/GID mismatches; confirm ownership on the server and the client's effective UID. For Samba, common culprits include forgotten smbpasswd entries, incorrect smb. conf syntax, or closed ports 137, 138, 139, and 445. When Samba authentication fails, confirm the user exists on the Linux system, that you ran sudo smbpasswd -a username, and that the share's valid users or write list settings include the account. Logs are your friend: check /var/log/syslog or Samba logs under /var/log/samba for detailed errors. Another frequent mistake is relying solely on IP-based restrictions for security. IPs can change or be spoofed; combine export restrictions with authentication and least privilege. A practical diagnostic flow: confirm network, confirm server exports or share visibility, check authentication credentials, inspect filesystem permissions, and finally review logs for specific error messages.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we explore two essential network file systems you will use as an LFCE: NFS for Unix-native sharing, and Samba to serve Windows clients. You will learn practical server and client steps, how to secure shares, and how to diagnose common permission and connectivity problems. NFSv4 simplifies firewall configuration by using port 2049 and offers stateful behavior; Samba implements SMB/CIFS so Linux servers can present Windows-style file and print services. We'll walk through configuration files you must master: /etc/exports for NFS and /etc/samba/smb. conf for Samba, plus the key commands like exportfs and smbpasswd. You will also see concrete examples for public and secured shares, mounting commands and fstab entries, and the security tradeoffs of options such as no_root_squash. Understanding these tradeoffs matters because misconfigured network shares open data to unauthorized users or can break applications that expect root access. Begin by understanding the roles each protocol plays. NFS is designed for Unix-like systems and provides a native filesystem semantics familiar to Linux administrators. It tends to be faster in homogeneous Linux fleets and integrates with Unix permissions, UID/GID mapping, and advanced features like Kerberos for strong authentication. Samba implements the SMB/CIFS protocol to serve Windows clients. Samba exposes shares that Windows expects—network drive mapping, Windows ACLs if configured, and simple guest access. A practical decision rule is: if your clients are primarily Linux servers or you need POSIX semantics, favor NFSv4; if you must support Windows workstations or mixed environments, use Samba. There are important contrasts to watch for. NFSv4 uses port 2049 and can be integrated with id mapping and Kerberos, which changes how permissions are enforced. Samba uses ports 139 and 445 and relies on smbpasswd or domain membership for authentication. Misconceptions often arise: some assume NFS is always insecure because it uses IP-based access by default; while true for simple setups, NFSv4 can be integrated with Kerberos for mutual authentication and encryption. Another misconception is that Samba is only for Windows; Samba serves Linux clients too via CIFS mounts. When planning, consider client mix, performance needs, and the authentication model you require.

Setting up an NFSv4 server is a short sequence of repeatable steps you will use in production. Start by installing the server package: on Debian/Ubuntu use the nfs-kernel-server package; on RHEL/CentOS use nfs-utils. Create a directory you intend to share, for example /srv/nfs/shared_data, and set ownership and permissions appropriate to the workload. The core configuration lives in /etc/exports. Each export line defines the path, the allowed clients, and options such as rw, sync, no_subtree_check, and root_squash/no_root_squash. After editing /etc/exports run exportfs -ra to reload export rules without restarting the server, and use systemctl restart nfs-server to restart the NFS service if needed. Open the NFS port in your firewall so authorized clients can reach port 2049. The /etc/exports file defines what a server shares and how clients may interact with those shares. Each line names a directory and one or more client specifications with options. Common options you will use immediately include rw for read/write, sync to force writes to disk before confirming to the client, no_subtree_check to avoid subtree permission checks for moved files, and root_squash which maps client root to an anonymous user on the server. That last option is particularly important: by default root_squash enhances server safety by preventing a root user on a client from having root privileges on the server. If an application on the client requires root-level access to the exported files, administrators may use no_root_squash, but they must do so only for trusted clients and after considering other protections like Kerberos and firewall controls. A typical production export will limit allowed clients by IP and avoid giving blanket access to all addresses. Remember to run exportfs -ra after editing /etc/exports to apply rules immediately. Misconfigurations often come from overly permissive client wildcards or forgetting to reload exports after changes.

After editing /etc/exports, the exportfs command synchronizes the kernel's export table with your configuration. The command sudo exportfs -ra re-exports all entries and applies changes immediately; it is a lightweight alternative to restarting the entire NFS service. In cases where the NFS server package or kernel module needs a restart, use systemctl restart nfs-server. For firewall configuration ensure that port 2049 is reachable from trusted clients. If using UFW, a simple rule might be sudo ufw allow from to any port nfs; with firewalld use sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=nfs and reload. Remember that older NFS versions used multiple RPC ports, but NFSv4 consolidates most traffic over 2049, simplifying firewall rules. After exporting, verify using sudo exportfs -v to list exported directories and options, and test mounts from a client. A common operational pitfall is reloading exports but forgetting the firewall rule, which leaves clients unable to connect even though the export exists. Security for NFS revolves around two ideas: identity mapping and authentication. Basic NFS relies on client-supplied UID and GID; that means ownership on the server is determined by numeric IDs. If users have different numeric IDs across hosts, permission problems follow. To address this, administrators keep consistent UIDs/GIDs across systems, or use mapping services such as idmapd in NFSv4 to map names properly. For stronger authentication and encryption, NFSv4 supports Kerberos integration. Kerberos provides mutual authentication so clients and servers can verify each other's identity, and it enables data integrity and privacy services. In enterprise deployments Kerberos is often required because IP-based access control and UID/GID consistency are not sufficient on their own. Remember, Kerberos setup requires a key distribution center and proper principal configuration; it is a deeper configuration step but critical for production security. A common misconception is that UID/GID mismatches are rare; they are frequent in environments with ad-hoc user creation. Always verify numeric IDs and consider idmapd or Kerberos if you need identity fidelity and cryptographic protection. Samba exposes Windows-compatible shares configured in /etc/samba/smb. conf. The file has a global section for server-wide settings and individual share sections enclosed in square brackets. To create a public share, add a section like [public] with path, browseable, read only, and guest ok parameters. Samba uses local Linux user accounts by default; you must create a Samba password for each user with smbpasswd -a username before they can authenticate. Samba can also join an Active Directory domain when needed for enterprise integration. For a practical example, a public share might force files to be created as nobody to prevent privilege escalation, while an authenticated share maps to real user accounts for accountability. Performance tuning for NFS and Samba focuses on balancing throughput and safety. For NFS tuning, client mount options rsize and wsize control the read and write block sizes; larger values can improve throughput on reliable networks. The sync option in an export forces data to disk before acknowledging writes, which ensures integrity but reduces write performance. The async option increases speed but risks data loss on a server crash. For Samba tuning, socket options like TCP_NODELAY, SO_RCVBUF, and SO_SNDBUF can help when you need to tweak network buffering; parameters like min receivefile size and getwd cache also influence performance. Across both systems network factors — latency, bandwidth, and NIC configuration — often dominate. Practical optimizations include using dedicated network interfaces for storage traffic, enabling jumbo frames where the network supports them, and isolating storage traffic from general-purpose networks. Always benchmark changes in a controlled environment; apply one change at a time and measure throughput and latency. A common pitfall is turning on async for NFS without understanding the crash recovery implications. When in doubt, prefer safe defaults and tune only after profiling real workloads.

Troubleshooting network file systems starts with a small checklist. If a client cannot mount a share, verify network reachability and firewall rules first. For NFS, ensure port 2049 is reachable and that exportfs -v shows the export. If mounts succeed but reads or writes fail with permission denied, check root_squash behavior and UID/GID mismatches; confirm ownership on the server and the client's effective UID. For Samba, common culprits include forgotten smbpasswd entries, incorrect smb. conf syntax, or closed ports 137, 138, 139, and 445. When Samba authentication fails, confirm the user exists on the Linux system, that you ran sudo smbpasswd -a username, and that the share's valid users or write list settings include the account. Logs are your friend: check /var/log/syslog or Samba logs under /var/log/samba for detailed errors. Another frequent mistake is relying solely on IP-based restrictions for security. IPs can change or be spoofed; combine export restrictions with authentication and least privilege. A practical diagnostic flow: confirm network, confirm server exports or share visibility, check authentication credentials, inspect filesystem permissions, and finally review logs for specific error messages.

Let's summarize the most important ideas. First, NFSv4 is the recommended Unix-native network file system; it uses port 2049 and can be integrated with Kerberos and id mapping for secure, consistent identity. Second, Samba implements SMB/CIFS so Linux servers can serve Windows clients; configure shares in /etc/samba/smb. conf and manage users with smbpasswd or domain membership. Third, /etc/exports is the authoritative policy file for NFS; options like sync and root_squash control durability and privilege, while exportfs -ra applies changes. Finally, performance and security choices are tradeoffs: sync versus async, rsize/wsize tuning, and whether to permit no_root_squash. Always apply least privilege, limit client IPs where possible, and verify mounts and permissions with simple file operations and logs. These are the foundational concepts you will return to when building shared storage in production.

Third, permissions issues often stem from identity mismatches—UID/GID differences for NFS and missing smbpasswd entries for Samba.
